The rally was the result of less negative macroeconomic data, stronger equity prices, ongoing Chinese buying and tight scrap supply. However, during the second half of the month fear over the potential effects of swine flu, amongst other things, contributed to a downtrend in official 3-month quotes. Some of the heightened buying has been in order to replenish inventories which were drawn down to very low levels during Q4 last year. It is also generally perceived that apart from replenishing depleted metal stocks with cheap copper units, the SRB may also be buying commodities in order to diversify out of US Treasuries and dollar holdings. China is, for example, reportedly concerned about the US Federal Reserve engineering a covert default on its debt by printing money. (See page 5)_ - _The key effect of the ongoing Chinese buying interest has been for copper prices to be boosted artificially and, although this has provided a welcome respite to the mining sector in the short term, this may have less advantageous consequences for the industry further out. _MSVMCU0904_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ ### **MARKET DEVELOPMENTS** _Copper prices during April followed two distinctive trading trends_ _Prices supported during the first half of the month…_ _.. on the back of positive economic news_ _.. and rising equities…_ During the first half of April official 3-month quotes rose on a daily basis, barring the 7th , from the month’s low of $4004/t on the 1st to a new 6-month high of $4770/t on the 15th . The $766/t (+19%) rally was the largest gain since February 2008 and was mainly the result of less negative macroeconomic data, stronger equity prices, ongoing Chinese buying and tight scrap supply. However, during the second half of the month fear over the potential effects of swine flu, amongst other things, contributed to a downtrend in official 3-month quotes. At the time of writing official 3-month prices traded at $4306/t on the 27th , down 9.7% (-$464/t) from the month’s peak of $4770/t. For the month-to-date (through to the 29th ) 3-month prices averaged $4415/t, up 16.7% from March’s average of $3784/t, while average cash prices rose by 17.4% to $4400/t. LME open interest data showed that both new long positions and short covering contributed to rising prices during the first two weeks of the month. Between the 1st and 6th LME open interest rose by 6.5k lots which, in conjunction with a $305/t gain in price, indicated the establishment of new long positions. As sentiment began to improve those “short” quickly rushed to cover their positions. This was highlighted by LME open interest data, between the 7th and 15th , falling by 6.1k lots alongside a $435/t increase in price. On the economic front market sentiment received a boost from the news that world leaders had agreed to commit to $1Tn in emergency stimulus at the recent G20 meetings. Sentiment was encouraged further by the announcement that Japan will double the size of its stimulus package. Added to this was the release of less negative economic data. In the US, the rise in factory orders was better than expected while in China, the official Purchasing Managers Index rose from 48.4 in February to 52.4 in March. Meanwhile in the construction sector, Chinese floor space under construction rose by 14.1% during the first two months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008. Finally in Japan, machine orders in March were up by 1.4% month on month versus an expected monthly decline of 6.9%. This was viewed as positive because machine orders are a leading economic indicator. Further price support came from the general market perception that the global economy is close to bottom and unlikely to deteriorate much further. This belief resulted in equity markets and base

_Page 2_ _April 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ Historically the movements in equity prices and base metals were poorly correlated. This lack of correlation has been a major factor in the popularity of commodities as an asset class as they can help diversify investment portfolios. However, if the S&P500 equity index is compared with the LME Price Index a switch from no correlation to a strong correlation has developed in the wake of the Lehman Brothers collapse. Both equity and base metal prices fell as investors were forced to sell a wide variety of assets to meet margin calls, debt repayment and redemptions. In the November 2008 to February 2009 period this correlation disappeared, but re-emerged in March with the belief that the global economy is bottoming out and downside risk is limited, encouraging investors into equities and base metals alike. _Historically no correlation between equities and base metals_ It is difficult to say when the inverse correlation between base metals and equities will return and whether this will take the form of base metal prices falling relative to equities or vice versa. On the one hand, the feeble state of metal demand in most regions that has been evidenced by economic data and steel prices, not helped by the forthcoming Northern Hemisphere summer slowdown, will act as a drag on prices. On the other hand, if investors believe that the current actions by governments to stimulate growth will provide a meaningful boost in metals demand and may in 12-24 months time even prove inflationary, then their interest in commodities is likely to be maintained both from a fundamental perspective and as a hedge against inflation. On the fundamental side Chinese buying was the major factor that pushed prices higher during the first half of the month (SHFE prices traded an average $487/t (net of VAT) above LME quotes during the first two weeks of the month). Although the arbitrage narrowed during week three, month-to-date (as of the 29th ) SHFE prices averaged $441/t above LME quotes. This compared with an average SHFE/LME arbitrage of $203/t in March, $222/t in February and $214/t in January. In recent years the favourable SHFE arbitrage has disappeared by mid February and thus in 2009 it has remained in place for considerably longer, implying that refined imports will continue to be sizeable in the coming months. Latest trade data showed Chinese refined copper imports increased by 138% in March year on year, to a new monthly record of 297kt. In addition to the favourable arbitrage in February the surge in March imports was also due to ti

The extent of the tightness was highlighted by official trade data which showed Chinese imports of copper scrap falling by 47.6% (-664kt gross weight) in Q1 from a year earlier. On a contained basis this equated to a loss of ~150kt Cu. _Chinese selling dampened sentiment_ _Exchange stocks continued to decline_ _European premia rates supported by demand from China…_ _.. likewise in the US_ While Chinese buying played a major part in supporting prices during the first half of the month Chinese selling, or rather rumours of SRB selling, dampened market sentiment during the second half of the month. Another contributing factor relates to growing concerns over what effect the recent outbreak of swine flu will have on any global economic recovery. The reversal in sentiment was highlighted by LME open interest data which showed that long liquidation and the development of new short positions pulled official prices (3m) down to $4355/t on the 24th . Prices thereafter recovered somewhat having traded around $4500/t at month’s end. Total exchange stocks continued to fall during the month. Through to the 29th they were down by a net 104.4kt to 464.4kt. LME inventories declined by a net 96kt, to 405.8kt, SHFE stocks fell by a net 10.1kt to 15.1kt while Comex inventories increased by a net 1.7kt to 43.6kt. On the LME net withdrawals were recorded on a daily basis barring the 1st, 3rd and the 7th . The largest withdrawals were from European locations where inventories declined by a net 80kt to 138kt. The majority of this material seems destined for China where higher prices and a higher premium can be achieved. We expect a further decline in LME inventories over the coming weeks because cancelled warrants remain at high levels. As of the 29th these totaled 64kt, up by 54.6kt from March. European physical premia remained firm during the month. However, this reflected buying activity from China rather than any pick up in European demand. Traders reported disappointing European demand in a quarter that is traditionally very busy.

Thus Chilean and Grade A material from Rotterdam continued to trade between $40-50/t while Italian warrants moved higher by $10-20/t to $50-70/t. Elsewhere, the ongoing tightness in the scrap market resulted in standard grade material trading up from -$20/t to level in March to level to $10/t at the end of the month. Likewise in the US, premia were pushed higher amid tighter scrap availability following extensive Chinese buying. Another contributing factor was that cathode that would normally be shipped from South America to the US was diverted to China because of the higher premia. Thus US premia rose from between 3.5c/lb and 4.5c/lb in March, to 5-6c/lb currently. Meanwhile in China, premia strengthened further, rising from $150/t in March to a peak of $160/t during the early part of April. However, we hear that premia have eased recently and are now trading closer to last month’s level. The high level of Chinese imports in recent months has reflected earlier buying from the State Reserves Bureau (SRB) and ongoing demand from consumers, particularly those that are short of scrap. Some of the heightened buying has been in order to replenish inventories which were drawn down to very low levels during Q4 last year. Some end-users have been able to increase their working inventories, from as low as 1 stock day to 5-7 days. Modest improvements in certain domestic market sectors and better availability of credit since the start of the year have also facilitated these purchases. Likewise, the SRB continues to take delivery of tonnages that were booked earlier in the year. It is generally perceived that apart from replenishing depleted metal stocks with cheap copper units, the SRB (or other government entities) may also be buying metals (including gold) as a means of diversifying out of US Treasuries and US dollar holdings. China is, for example, reportedly concerned about the US Federal Reserve engineering a covert default on its debt by printing money. The key effect of the ongoing Chinese buying interest has been to boost copper prices artificially and, although this has provided a welcome respite to the mining sector in the short term, this may have less advantageous consequences for the industry further out. This is because the market has not had a chance to correct properly

with supply continuing to exceed physical demand. At the same time, there is far less incentive for marginal producers to shut down. Today’s prices are 60% higher than last year’s low of $2800/t and provide an ideal opportunity for high cost miners to hedge their production at price levels that will ensure their survival even if future spot prices tumble. Also, at today’s levels some producers have been encouraged to reopen. An example of this is Camec’s Luita mine (30kt/a) in the DRC which may see the start of an increasing trend, as has happened in the zinc market. Also, some mines which were due to close will now remain open, e.g. Mopani’s Mufulira and Nkana mines. Because of these factors, we have reduced the production lost in our mine closure/curtailment list from 750kt/a Cu to 600kt currently. _Recent Chinese interest reflected buying from consumers and the SRB_ _Chinese interest created artificial price rise_ COPPER SPOT PREMIUMS

_April 2009_ _Page 5_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ _Prices may trade in a much narrower range_ _Potential for huge price correction once the SRB exit_ _Our price forecast are unchanged from last month_ As has been suggested in various press reports it is not inconceivable that the SRB etc. will continue to “buy the price dips” and stockpile even larger amounts of metal (there has been talk, for example, of overall purchases of between 700kt to 1Mt for this year). Under such a scenario prices are unlikely to reach the lows seen in December last year. Were this buying to continue then these non-commercial metal purchases would at some point become available to the market with the potential of significantly dampening any fundamentally driven future price hike. The flip side to this is that China becomes increasingly weighed down by arbitrage-related copper purchases (metal and possibly scrap), with ballooning inventories on account of domestic consumers struggling to keep pace with imports and output from local producers and with the SRB losing its appetite to make further purchases. Under this scenario (which we believe is quite possible) the market will rapidly run out of steam in the sense that buying momentum will be lost and that, in the absence of a meaningful pick up in consumption, particularly in the mature economies, inventories will start to increase again. It is perhaps worth mentioning that Chinese demand does not appear as strong as some of the official data suggests. According to the CNIA, Chinese copper semis output increased by 12.7% in Q1 from a year ago (though the NBS points to a 1% decline). We have difficulty reconciling the robust rate of growth noted by the CNIA with other indicators. For example, end-u

se data showed either very small or negative growth during Q1 while latest trade data indicated that demand from overseas was also well down (see Consumption). In addition, power generating capacity, the major end use market for copper, increased by only 10GW in Q1. On an annualised basis this is running 50% behind the forecast addition rate (80GW) for this year. We have left our price forecasts for this year unchanged at $3636/t ($1.65/lb) which implies lower prices during H2 2009. ### **CONSUMPTION** 

With the exception of China, demand for copper around the globe remains exceptionally weak.  The downturn in copper’s main end-use markets, namely construction, automotive and electrical and electronic products, continues to impact negatively on demand.  This is particularly true of the auto sector where General Motors (GM) in the US recently announced that it will reduce production by closing 13 assembly plants for as long as nine weeks.  Meanwhile in Japan the output of rolled copper products fell by a record 60% in March from a year earlier, according to the Japan Copper and Brass Association.  As a consequence we forecast that demand this year will decline in every country barring China, dropping by 8.2% to just under 11.9Mt.  Including China we forecast that global demand, overall, will fall by 3.7% this year to 17.3Mt.  In 2010 we do not expect any recovery in demand outside of China where refined consumption is forecast to fall by a further 0.7% to 11.8Mt.  Taking China into account, however, we project that global demand will increase by 1.5%, to just under 17.6Mt, before growing by a much stronger 6.3% in 2011 to 18.7Mt.

The sharp deterioration in Japanese business sentiment was highlighted recently by the Bank of Japan’s latest Tankan survey (March) which showed the diffusion index for supply and demand among large manufacturers falling to minus 59.  This was down 25 points from the previous survey in December and represented the lowest reading since February 1976.  Companies have been trimming excess labour and capital spending for some time now but the results from the tankan survey indicated that the drop in demand was much larger than the companies anticipated, thereby rekindling fears of overcapacity.  This is particularly true of the auto sector where auto production declined by 49% during the first two months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008. Activity within the housing sector was not much better where housing starts fell by 25% year on year during the first two months of the year. 

Reflecting falling orders from the auto sector, as well as the semi-conductor sector, several copper strip manufacturers suspended production from October last year.  As a consequence the Japan Brass Makers Association reported a 66.7% year on year drop in production during the first two months of 2009. Demand for bronze sheet and strip also declined dramatically during the twomonth period with output down 76.7% year on year.  This reflected weak orders for mobile phones, digital cameras, personal computers and other electrical items.  Elsewhere the poor performing housing sector took its toll on demand for copper tube and bras

s bar where production declined annually by 32.4% and 40.3% respectively through to February. Overall the Japan Brass Makers Association reported a 52% year on year decline in the production of copper and copper alloy products during the first two months of 2009. As mentioned earlier the Association reported a further 62.6% year on year decline in production in March, to just 32.3kt. For Q1 as a whole, output of copper and copper alloy products declined by 55.7% from a year earlier. The wire and cable markets are not performing well either. According to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association wire and cable shipments in February fell 32.4% year on year to their lowest level since August 1975. All market sectors recorded annual declines with the largest falls seen in the automotive (-59.6%), electrical and electronic (-50.5%) and construction sectors (21.5%). The sharp decline in shipments to the automotive sector, which represented the largest monthly year on year drop ever, reflected plunging orders for automotive winding wire in light of falling auto production. In the electrical and electronic sector deliveries were down because of reduced facility investment by both heavy machinery manufacturers and producers of electrical home appliances. The reduction in the construction of buildings and plants was also partly responsible for shipments of power cable declining by 9% year on year. The other factor was a lower requirement for electricity transmission facilities. Finally, shipments to the telecommunication sector declined by 4.4% year on year because of reduced facility investment for copper cables by NTT. The Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association recently reported that wire and cable shipments declined by a further 25% in March from a year earlier, indicating that the slowdown in wire and cable demand continues unabated. With this in mind, alongside the sharp downturn in demand for copper and copper alloy products, we continue to forecast that Japanese refined copper consumption will decline by 15.8% this year to just above 1Mt. Demand has not been this low since 1975, according to our records. Meanwhile in the USA, economic indicators published for March showed that while the economy continued to shrink there were some tentative signs of stability. According to the Purchasing Managers In

dex manufacturing activity contracted for the 14th consecutive month in March. However, at 36.3 it was 0.5% higher than February’s reading. More encouraging was the new orders index which rose above 40% for the first time in seven months and 8.1% from a month earlier. Small signs of revival have also been seen in areas of the housing market which have been devastated by the downturn. The interest rate for a 30-year fixed rate loan fell to a 38-year low making it cheaper in some cities to buy rather than, thus bringing new house buyers to the market. The outlook should improve further when the effect of the Obama administration’s housing market stimuli, in the form of loan modifications and other props, come into force. However, these positive steps are only possible due to the large amounts of government money being pumped into the housing sector. This is not a viable long term strategy and with unemployment in March at 8.5%, a 25-year high, and consumers cautious about spending after their savings have been demolished by the recent stock market crash, it seems a genuine rise in demand is a long way off. _April 2009_ _Page 9_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ _US auto sector continued to deteriorate dramatically_ _..which is reflected in US demand for copper and copper alloy products…_ _.. and wire and cable demand_ According to latest government statistics US car and light vehicle production totalled 1.2M units in Q1 2009, 54% lower than the comparable quarter of 2008, and 35% lower than in Q4 2008. The Q1 output gives a projected annualised level for the year of 4.8M units, down from 8.7M units last year. However output did pick up quite considerably in March, at 476k units, compared with 412k units in February and just 289k units in January. Nevertheless, any hint of positive market sentiment that could be drawn from this is likely to be severely dented by the announcement from GM in late April that it will reduce production over the next three months to lower its inventory of cars and trucks and avoid the risk of an uncontrolled shutdown from the financial crisis at bankrupt supplier Delphi Corp. By closing 13 assembly plants for as long as nine weeks the company will cut its North American production by 190k units through Q2 and Q3. Elsewhere time is running out for Chrysler to comply with a number of government requirements which will prevent the company from en

tering bankruptcy. Chrysler has until April 30th to secure an alliance with Italian car producer Fiat, reach agreements with its banks to reduce debt and agree labour cost reductions with its unions. The downturn in both the auto and construction sectors continues to impact negatively on the demand for copper. The American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) recently reported a 34.1% year on year decline in the production of copper and copper alloy products in January. Unsurprisingly copper tube was particularly weak, with output falling by 35.4% from a year earlier to ~21kt. As if to underscore the dire market conditions, Mueller Industries, a major copper semis manufacturer, reported that its net sales in Q1 fell by 54% from the corresponding period in 2008. The company reported that ~60% of the decline in sales was due to lower demand from the OEM (original equipment manufacturer) segment. - Elsewhere in the wire and cable markets demand for copper wire rod continued to decline sharply during the first two months of the year. The ABMS reported a 24.3% year on year fall in production during the two-month period from a year earlier. Taking all of the above into account we forecast that US refined copper consumption will decline by 10% this year to ~1.8Mt, its lowest level since 1983. |**PRODUCTION AN**|**D SHIPM**

confuse. According to the CNIA the output of copper and copper alloy products rose by 12.7% year on year in Q1. The rate of growth appeared very strong when compared with production data for end use goods. For example, according to the National Bureau of Metal Statistics the production of household air conditioners declined by 28% in Q1 from a year earlier, the production of power generating equipment fell by 25.5% year on year while the output of electric motors dropped by 16.7% from the corresponding period in 2008. Elsewhere the production of refrigerators, washing machines and motor vehicles increased by 7.9%, 4.7% and 3.7% respectively during Q1 year on year. This compared with double-digit annual growth in all these products during Q1 last year. The sharp rise in semis output did not reflect strong demand from overseas either. Trade data showed that during Q1 exports of copper semi products fell by 40% (-54kt) in Q1 from a year earlier. The decline largely reflected a 35% (-52kt) fall in demand for copper tube. This was not unexpected in light of the chronic slowdown in the global construction sector. Added to the confusion was the release of data from the National Bureau of Statistics which reported a 1% decline in the output of copper and copper alloy products during Q1 from a year earlier. The CNIA growth figure could be overstated because of double counting and increased production resulting from increased market share rather than any improvement in fresh demand. However, it would be difficult to expect these factors to fully explain the disparity between the CNIA and NBS figures. Our Chinese sources indicated that there was minimal growth in copper semis demand during Q1 this year, which implied that the NBS negative growth of 1% is more indicative of current market conditions. This is also in line with our forecast growth of 2% in the production of copper and copper alloy products this year. On a primary basis we forecast a 7.9% increase in Chinese refined consumption this year to ~5.4Mt. This brings the first quarter tally to 1.41Mdmt, which is equivalent to a 3.2% uplift over the same period in 2008. There has been a sizeable shift in the contribution to this latter total on a country-by-country basis with, for example, Chile’s market share declining from 35% to 22% currently. The

reduction reflects lower shipments from various operations, with Collahuasi and Escondida being the most notable. Elsewhere, Peru’s relative significance has increased, from 12% to 18%, with the most important contributors being Antamina, Cerro Verde and Cuajone/Toquepala.  Other noteworthy gains were recorded from countries such as Laos (+70kt), Iran (+33kt) and Kazakhstan (+33kt). 

As noted, after a fairly brisk start to the month Chinese spot buying interest has waned somewhat, although this may be more related to a narrowing of the SHFE:LME price arbitrage than a tailing off of consumer requirements.  Indeed, Jiangxi Copper is still active in the spot market and is aggressively seeking tonnage.  Other smelting companies are also likely to be back in the market in due course, including Dongying and Yunnan Copper. 

Japanese smelters recently announced their production intentions for the period April to September 2009.  Plans call for an overall year-on-year reduction in refined copper output of 3.2%, i.e. down from 750.4kt to 737.1kt.  PPC will lower output at its Saganoseki smelter by 7.3% to 198.5kt while its share of Tamano production will increase by 6.9% to 91.8kt.  In reality, Tamano’s output isn’t due to change but the other partners will reduce their respective off take. Meanwhile, Sumitomo Metal Mining plans to produce 200kt during the period which is 7% lower than its original budget but still 20.6% higher in comparison with the same time last year.  Mitsubishi Materials is to maintain the 10% cut that it announced earlier this year and aims to produce 145.6kt from its Naoshima smelter and its near-half share from Onahama.  However, some of this cut is beyond Mitsubishi Material’s control because, as mentioned last month, the Onahama smelter has been operating at 75% of capacity since a fire broke out on March 12<sup>th</sup> .  According to local press sources the repairs could take up to four months to complete.  Dowa Mining forecasts a 23% drop in output to 40.2kt (the company has a 30% share in Onahama plus a small amount of production at its Kosaka plant).  Furukawa Mining projects a 12% decline (to 41.4kt) from its share of Tamano and Onahama quotas while Nittetsu Mining’s share from Tamano will be 21% lower (19.7kt) than the same period last year.

and reversal of closure decisions_ 

Last month we highlighted the fact that there had been a noticeable tail off in mine closure announcements.  Since then, under a higher price environment, one mine has actually been reactivated while the suspension decisions for two others have been retracted.  The recent recovery in cobalt and copper prices has led to the reopening of Camec’s DRC copper and cobalt operations, including the Disele mine and the Luita SxEw copper/cobalt facility.  Last year’s production was less than 10kt Cu, although Camec’s current capacity is ~30kt/a Cu and the operation continues to be expanded in 10kt/a modules with a view to raising production to 100kt/a.  Elsewhere, south of the DRC border, rising copper prices have resulted in Mopani Copper reversing its earlier decision to suspend production at its 60kt/a Mufulira mine and its 50kt/a Nkana mine.  Weatherly International is also considering reopening its Namibian mines (Matchless, Otjihase etc.) later this year and is looking for a joint-venture partner to assist in this process.  Various companies are now taking the opportunity to hedge their output (Inmet Mining, Lundin Mining, Taseko Mines etc.) to capitalise on this latest price hike.

Grupo Mexico has received clearance from the Mexican Labour Ministry’s Conciliation and Arbitration Board to close its 170kt/a Cananea mine. This is a significant move because it potentially allows the company to pay off the existing workforce, rehire workers under a more moderate union and repair damages to the plant and equipment. However, this may not be a particularly rapid process given that the existing union is likely to challenge the decision and in any event repairs and retraining programmes etc. will take time to complete. The mine was shut down in April 2008 having produced only 6.2kt of copper in concentrates and 9.4kt of SxEw Cu in that year. Production at Konkola Copper Mines’ new 300kt/a Nchanga smelter remains idled following a fire at the plant that halted production on April 6th . Initial indications suggest that there had been an internal explosion in the prime smelting furnace in the area of a water cooled tap block. The smelter is unusual in that there are no converters which is due to the unusually low sulphur and iron content of the Konkola concentrates. Current estimates suggest that operations will resume during the first half of May. China’s Ningbo Jintian resumed production at its 200kt/a refinery in Zhejiang province after a three-month closure on account of a shortage of scrap. The plant was shut down in December 2008 having produced only 104.3kt during the year.
